title: ECMO Cart
content:
ECMO Cart Requirements

An ECMO cart is used for cannulation, reconfiguration, management of various complications, and decannulation in any non-operating room setting. Review the requirements then select the equipment according to your ECMO needs.
  • The items included MUST be immediately available for the cannulating team.
  • The cart should be kept in a dedicated location when not in use.
  • The items in the cart and on top of the cart MUST be maintained. This means they MUST be checked for content and expiration dates, and refilled with used items, as per center policy.

title: Anticoagulation with Intravenous Unfractionated Heparin (UFH)
content: Use this checklist to guide the initiation and maintenance of intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH) anticoagulation following ECMO cannulation.
keywords: Anticoagulation; Heparin; Unfractionated Heparin; UFH; Anticoagulants; ECMO Cannulation; Intravenous; AntiXa; aPTT; Coagulation

items.label: ECMO Cannulation
UFH IV Bolus: 50-100 IU/kg
Consider dose according to coagulation status and bleeding risk.
Continuous Anticoagulation
Starting dose: 10-15 IU/kg /h using actual body weight (use adjusted body weight if BMI ≥ 40 kg/m<sup class="math-sup">2</sup>).
Maintenance dose will be determined based on the anticoagulation target for (according to local protocol, if available, coagulation status and bleeding risk)*:
Low: AntiXa 0.2-0.3 IU/mL and/or aPTT: 40-55s; ratio 1.2-1.6;
Moderate: AntiXa 0.3-0.5 IU/mL and/or aPTT: 50-70s; ratio 1.5-2;
High: AntiXa 0.5-0.7 IU/mL and/or aPTT: 60-80s; ratio 1.8-2.4.
Monitor anticoagulation parameters at least twice daily and after four hours after any dose adjustment.
Below target: increase UFH dose 10-20%^, check anticoagulation parameter after four hours.
Above target: decrease UFH dose 10-20%^, check anticoagulation parameter after four hours.
Discrepancy between aPTT and AntiXa: Refer to the Discrepancy between aPTT and AntiXa with UFH Table under Anticoagulants.
Daily assessment for Bleeding and Thromboembolism and HIT
Refer to Management of bleeding
Clotting in circuit

title: How to Salvage Blood in the ECMO Circuit
content: This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.
keywords: ECMO MANAGEMENT; BLOOD; CIRCUIT; SALVAGE; SUSPENSION TECHNIQUE; BUCKET TECHNIQUE; BLOOD SALVAGE; ECMO CIRCUIT

items.label: Bucket Technique (most effective)
In the surgical sterile field fill a large bowl with balanced electrolyte solution.
Submerge the ECMO venous drainage cannula in the bowl (make sure it stays submerged)
Direct the return ECMO cannula into an empty bowl, place the cell saver in the empty bowl (take the Yankauer tip off)
Remove the clamps and increase RPM slowly until blood flows into the cell saver bowl (typically 1000-1500 RPM is enough as there is very little resistance)
Stop once the blood is displaced from the circuit
This circuit may be kept on standby for a few hours and reused for the same patient if it is kept circulating and is otherwise useable
Suspension Technique
Attach a large-bore quick-prime line with fluids to a pre-pump pigtail; insert one if necessary.
Remove the venous cannula from the patient
Hold the cannula up in the air, remove the clamp
Slowly increase RPM until blood flows into the patient via the return cannula
Carefully watch the meniscus in the venous line, clamp below the fluid level just before it gets to pigtail
Open the fluid line and continue administering circuit blood to the patient
Stop if indicated hemodynamically or if the blood has all been displaced
A cell saver can be attached to a return line pigtail instead of directly transfusing it via the return cannula, if desired.

title: Cannula Exit Sites and Tubings Management
content: This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.
keywords: CANNULA; EXIT SITE; TUBING MANAGEMENT; CANNULA MANAGEMENT; ACCIDENTAL DECANNULATION

items.label: General Care
Well-secure the cannulas with stitches or sutures devices according to the institutional protocol.
Use a 2 to 3-point securing strategy to stabilize tubings using available devices (tubing holders, catheter holders, self-adhering bandage, tape, etc.) adapted to the insertion site.
Avoid unnecessary manipulation.

Carefully avoid any traction on tubings/cannula during mobilization, transports, and physical therapy. Consider having a dedicated person for lines and tubing through patient movement, e.g., pressure area care and transportation of the patient.

At least once per shift, measure the length of the exposed portion of the cannula from the insertion site to a point clearly and univocally discussed/shared with the whole team (e.g., end of wire-reinforced portion, holding ring, PC connector, etc.). If there is any major mobilization or any doubt of a potential displacement, repeat the measurement.

Compare the exposed portion measurement with the previous one. If there is greater than a 5 mm difference for adults, 3mm for children or 2mm in neonates patients, discuss the need for diagnostic exams (ultrasonography and/or radiography) with the ECMOlogist. A minimal difference could be related to an evolving edema.
At least once per shift, observe exit sites or bleeding through the dressing if transparent OR
Observe exit sites during dressing replacement. If complications are detected, increase monitoring frequency. Carefully look for:
Integrity of the perilesional skin
Integrity of the anchoring sutures, if any OR integrity of sutureless devices
Signs of bleeding
Signs of non hemorrhagic oozing
Signs of infection/inflammation: report to the ECMOlogist and discuss the need to perform a wound swab
Perform routine dressing replacement for central venous access device (CVAD) dressings based on the dressing type, institutional policies, and current clinical guidelines
Perform unscheduled dressing changes immediately if the current dressing becomes compromised, loose, or soiled
Use an aseptic technique when replacing cannula dressing
Select the antiseptic solution for the cannula exit sites according to the most recent guidelines for CVADs management and to institutional policies when replacing the cannula dressing
Avoid direct and prolonged contact between PC connectors and alcohol-based antiseptic solutions
When replacing dressings or holders/tapes, stabilize the cannula or the tubing with on-hand
Remove the dressing toward the exit site—NOT toward the tubing

If there are any inexperienced staff at the bedside (e.g., students, new nurses or residents, etc.), quickly review the Accidental Decannulation protocol before leaving them alone for any reason or time
Care for Non-Oozing Exit Sites
Prefer transparent dressings
Consider impregnated transparent dressings as per institutional protocol
Care for Oozing Exit Sites
If bleeding is detected, consider hemostatic dressings as per institutional protocol

If there is persistent or major bleeding, apply pressure and discuss the need for a surgical consult/wound revision and adapting the anticoagulation strategy/assess coagulopathic state with the ECMOlogist
If fresh clots form over a previously bleeding exit site, avoid removal to restart the bleeding
If there are old clots over a previously bleeding exit site, carefully remove them through rinsing to avoid restarting the bleeding
If there is no hemorrhagic oozing detected, consider an absorbent dressing as per institutional protocol
If there is a purulent discharge, consider need
Signs of Accidental Decannulation
If there are ANY signs of accidental decannulation, this is an emergency. Refer to Accidental Decannulation
Documentation
Report on the exit site appearance
Report exposed portion measurements
Record any anomaly/complication
Report any dressing replacement if performed by specifying the type
Report any other procedure as cannula position monitoring, sampling for cultures
Latest monitoring completed/responsible ECMO specialist/perfusionist
If this is the case, update the ELSO registry

title: Elective ECMO Circuit Change
content: This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.
keywords: Elective ECMO Circuit Change; CIRCUIT CHANGE; ELECTIVE; PROCEDURE; ECMO MANAGEMENT

items.label: Risk/Benefit Considerations
When an ECMO circuit is no longer able to provide adequate support or becomes a significant potential risk to the patient, an elective ECMO Circuit Change should be planned
Postponing an ECMO Circuit Change may unnecessarily place the patient at risk of additional complications
Unnecessary ECMO Circuit Changes should be avoided due to patient risks outlined below as well as to avoid unnecessary resource burdens
If perceived ECMO circuit problem can be safely resolved by an isolated small component change, discuss component change rather than ECMO circuit change
If perceived ECMO circuit problem is the result of an issue with the cannulae, a circuit change itself will not resolve the problem
An ECMO circuit change may require additional blood product exposures, especially in neonatal/pediatric patients
An ECMO circuit change will dilute circulating medications
An ECMO Circuit Change results in additional foreign surface exposure and potentially an inflammatory response
Risk inherent with every ECMO Circuit Change:
Embolism
Infection
Instability or code during circuit change and sequelae of such
Procedural catastrophe
Indications
Consumptive Coagulopathy
Products consumed in ECMO circuit (positive feedback loop of coagulation) resulting in clotting within the ECMO circuit and usually a bleeding patient
Patient may present as in Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
This condition is diagnosed as profound and documented as increasing over a 12-hour period despite appropriate replacement products (FFP, Cryo, Platelets) and systemic anticoagulation
RULE OUT: surgical bleeding or coagulopathy not associated with the ECMO Circuit (dilutional, trauma, hypothermia)
Critical Hemolysis/Centrifugal Pump Thrombosis
Visualization or auditory confirmation of clot presence in centrifugal pump head
Critical plasma free hemoglobin (confirmed with a repeated result, no other symptoms necessary)
Elevated plasma free hemoglobin with clinical signs of hemolysis (hematuria, pink effluent)
Be cautious of false elevation of PFHB results
Draw technique
Hyperbilirubinemia
Hematochromatosis
Ferritin
Ancillary or other devices as source of hemolysis (Impella, CVVHD/CRRT)
Flow/cannula/shunt physiology as source of hemolysis as changing circuit will not eliminate these sources
Membrane Lung Dysfunction
Oxygenator Resistance
Increased resistance within the oxygenator (clot)
Evidenced by:
Decreasing flow over time with the centrifugal pump at the same or higher RPM and unchanged patient pre-load and afterload and cannula position verified
Increasing transmembrane pressure with constant flow and viscosity, continues to increase with subsequent drops in flows at increasing RPMs
Oxygenator Gas Transfer
Oxygen transfer significantly less than predicted by manufacturer
Note the effect of hemoglobin on the oxy-hemoglobin dissociation curve.
Note the effect of acidosis on oxy-hemoglobin dissociation curve.
Note the SvO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> of venous blood entering oxygenator.

Note that saturation is a much greater contributor to gas exchange than pO2; oxygen transfer can be estimated with pre-oxygenator saturation and post-oxygenator saturation if measured and the pO2 portion of the equation eliminated (no circuit gas draws needed if saturations are measured and trustworthy).

CO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> clearance significantly less than predicted by manufacturer, or unable to maintain physiologic PCO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> delivery on maximum sweep gas rate per manufacturer
Code Status and Consent
Ensure that an ECMO Circuit Change aligns with the patient’s goals of care

An elective ECMO Circuit Change should only proceed with a patient who is full code status given the significant potential for resuscitation to be required during the ECMO Circuit Change procedure (momentary cessation of ECMO). Patients with active Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR) orders must consent to rescind DNAR for the procedure
For elective ECMO Circuit Changes, consent should be obtained prior to proceeding

Roles

Run Code/Resuscitation if necessary
Perfusionist or ECMO Specialist:
Operate ECMO circuits and fill air-free connections
Sterile Perfusionist/ECMO Specialist/Physician/Provider:
Make sterile cuts and connections to the ECMO circuit

Manage the patient throughout the ECMO Circuit Change as needed and/or indicated
Preparations
Prepare a new ECMO circuit for initiation of support

Sterile person preps in ECMO lines/cannulas near where connections/cuts desired for ECMO circuit change using antiseptic with appropriate dry time and creating a sterile field with sterile drapes/towels.
New ECMO Circuit is clamped and handed up to the sterile field
A sterile person secures and prepares the new circuit by making any necessary cuts and inserting any needed connectors
A sterile person orients the new ECMO circuit and prepares clamps, scissors, and/or blades for easy accessibility
Timeout
Positive patient identification
Brief outline of roles and plan
Confirm emergency medications are prepared and who will deliver if needed
Confirm emergency airway or ventilator settings and who will operate
Confirm orientation of new ECMO circuit and preparedness of perfusionist/ECMO Specialist to cease ECMO flow on old circuit, fill air-free connections, and initiation ECMO on new circuit
Confirm sterile person has sterile scissors/blade, sterile clamps, any necessary connectors, and physiologic fill solution is ready
ECMO Circuit Change Procedure
During this procedure the primary care team manages patient care/resuscitation as clinically indicated
Sterile person loudly announces to room “Off ECMO” while clamping inflow and outflow lines—both proximal and distal—to desired cut/connection location
Sterile person either cuts lines or removes lines from cannula with great care to not score cannula connectors or disrupt cannula placement
Sterile person prepares to connect the new circuit to patient access/cannulae and instructs perfusionist/ECMO Specialist to “Fill” using the physiologic solution in a syringe or bulb syringe
Perfusionist/ECMO Specialist creates a steady stream of fluid to allow for air-free connection. Repeat for additional ECMO lines
Perfusionist/ECMO Specialist and Sterile person confirm directionality and air-free connections
Sterile person loudly announces to room “Go On ECMO”
Sterile person and Perfusionist/ECMO Specialist remove clamps from the new circuit and patient access/cannulae while Perfusionist/ECMO Specialist increases RPMs initiating ECMO Flow via new circuit
Team confirms adequacy of ECMO support, sends new labs, and requests imaging if any risk of cannula placement changes occurred, including if CPR was initiated at any point.

title: Circuit Component Changes
content: Use this checklist if you need to replace a component within an ECMO circuit. This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and  available resources.

items.label: Identify the need for circuit component replacement
To proceed with whole circuit replacement, all three checks are required. Otherwise, do NOT proceed with whole circuit replacement.
Note: ELSO does NOT recommend non-urgent replacement of a circuit or circuit component.
Dysfunctional circuit component: (at least 1 check)
Component thrombosis (minor membrane lung (ML) clotting not severely impacting with its function excluded).
Refer to Membrane Lung Failure.
Broken component
No weaning potential
Replacement of the whole circuit is not indicated
Refer to Whole Circuit Replacement.
OR
Need to switch to different configurations (e.g., VAV to VV or VA, VV-V to VV or VV to  VV-V, etc.)
Alert/activate the ECLS Team
Notify the ICU teams
1 experienced intensivist or other ECMO-trained physician
1 experienced ICU nurse to support the patient if as needed
1 experienced ICU nurse to support the patient if as needed
1 assisting ECMO specialist/perfusionist, if possible
If this is an elective procedure, consider having a short pre-procedure briefing.
Prepare the Essential Equipment
Refresh the team on techniques for air-free circuit connections.
Sterile consumables for "sterile operator"
Sterile tubing scissors
4 sterile tubing clamps
2 back-up sterile tubing clamps
1 sterile bowl
1 L of crystalloid solution
New component (CP, ML, tubing piece, connector)
2 straight connectors adapted to circuit tubing size
Disinfecting solution and/or applicators for tubings preparation (per institutional policy)
Devices for air-free connection
Large cone syringes OR
Pigtail/infusion bag OR
14G IV line
Prepare the Patient
Consider the following:
Supine the patient in same position as for initiation
If the patient is awake:
Inform him/her and/or their surrogate about the need for replacement, the procedure and potential associated risks (consent)
Consider sedation, if deemed necessary
Increase mechanical ventilation settings as ready to interrupt extracorporeal blood flow on VV ECMO, V-AV ECMO, VP ECMO
Increase inotropic/vasopressor support as ready to interrupt extracorporeal blood flow on VA ECMO, V-AV ECMO, VP ECMO
Be ready for PRBC transfusion if required
Be ready to perform CPR/ACLS if/as required in case of emergency
If the patient isn't on mechanical ventilation, be ready to manage airways in case of emergency
Check the coagulation profile and increase anticoagulant dosing if deemed necessary
Proceed with Replacement
Support the patient if/as needed throughout the procedure.
If cardiac arrest occurs during the procedure and EBF can be promptly restarted, carefully consider if adrenaline  administration is advisable or could be delayed.
Centrifugal Pump Replacement
Disinfect the portion of tubing which is going to be cut on both sides of the old centrifugal pump (CP).
Allow the solution to act for enough time according to the solution being used.
Clamp the tubing exiting CP.
Go to 0 RPMs and notify the team of the STOP FLOW.
Clamp the drainage tubing close to CP.
Turn OFF the Sweep Gas Flow (SGF).
Place two additional clamps approximately 15cm (6 inches) apart from the previous to isolate the CP from the circuit. If needed, temporarily remove the flowmeter.
Cut the tubings on both sides between the two clamps.
Remove the old centrifugal pump from the motor.
Connect the outflow of the new pump to the circuit.
De-air the new centrifugal pump through the inlet port.
Connect the inlet of the CP to the drainage tubing using an air-free technique. If previously removed, reposition and 0 the flowmeter.
Insert the CP into the motor. Check that there are no kinks or traction in the tubings on both sides.
Remove clamp on the drainage tubing.
Restart the pump.
As minimum RPMs are reached to prevent backflow, remove last clamp.
Refer to the Pump specifications.
Resume the previous RPMs settings if there are no signs of a return obstruction.
Go to Return Obstruction checklist.
Resume previous Sweep Gas Flow settings.
Notify the team of replacement completion.
If using a bubble sensor, and it is alarming for the presence of air before the membrane lung, consider removing through the de-airing port of the ML, without stopping the extracorporeal blood flow.
Refer to Air in Circuit for more information.
Membrane Lung Replacement
Remove Heater Unit/Heater-Cooler Unit lines from the old membrane lung (ML).
Disinfect the portion of tubing which is going to be cut on both sides of the old ML.
Allow the disinfection solution to act for enough time according to the solution being used.
Clamp the tubing exiting the ML.
Go to 0 RPMs and notify the team of the STOP FLOW.
Clamp tubing entering the old ML.
Turn OFF Sweep Gas Flow (SFG) and disconnect the gas line.
Place two additional clamps approximately 15 cm (six inches) apart from the previous to isolate the ML from the circuit.
If needed, temporarily remove the flowmeter.
Cut the tubing on both sides between the two clamps.
Remove the old ML from the holder.
Connect the outflow of the new pump to the circuit.
De-air the new centrifugal pump through the inlet port.
Connect the inlet of the CP to the drainage tubing using the air free technique (if previously removed reposition and 0 the flowmeter).
Insert the CP into the motor. Check for no kinks or traction in the tubings on both sides.
Remove clamp on drainage tubing.
Restart the pump at minimum RPMs reached to prevent backflow.
Depending on IFUs - Refer to the Pump specifications.
Remove the last clamp.
Resume previous RPMs settings, if there are no signs of a return obstruction.
Refer to Return Obstruction for more information.
Resume previous SGF settings.
Notify the team of procedure completion.
If using a bubble sensor, and it is alarming for the presence of air before the membrane lung, consider removing through the de-airing port of the ML, without stopping the extracorporeal blood flow.
Refer to Air in Circuit for more information.
Tubing/Connector Replacement
Disinfect the portion of tubing which is going to be cut.
Allow the disinfection solution to act for enough time according to the solution which has been used.
Clamp the tubing exiting the ML.
Go to 0 RPMs notifying to the team the STOP FLOW.
Clamp tubing entering the old ML.
Turn OFF SGF.
Place two additional clamps to isolate the portion which is going to be cut (three clamps if Y connector  included).
Cut the tubing between the two clamps.
Insert a straight or Y connector as needed in one of the tubing and connect the other/s portion using a wet-wet technique.
If a Y connector is used, connect to the Y connector a new piece of tubing, deair using a cone syringe and connect to the new cannula once all connections are ready.
Remove clamp on drainage tubing.
Restart the pump at minimum RPMs reached to prevent backflow.
Depending on IFUs - Refer to the Pump specifications.
Remove the last clamp.
Resume previous RPMs settings if there are no signs of a return obstruction.
Refer to Return Obstruction.
Resume previous SGF settings.
Notify the team of procedure completion.
Post-Replacement Management
Check all connections for tightness and integrity. Zip tie connections.
Closely monitor the patient for signs of complications.
Adjust ECMO settings as needed, considering improved function of the component, particularly if the ML has been changed.
Perform a full circuit assessment before leaving the patient.
Refer to Circuit Monitoring for additional information.
If the component change was due to an unexpected/unexplained malfunction, inform the manufacturer.
If the old components do not need to be returned to the manufacturer, dispose of them according to hospital protocol. Otherwise, store according to hospital protocol.
Document the procedure in the patient's chart, including:
Reason for replacement
Time of the procedure
Component/connectors lot numbers
Complications encountered
If any, operators
Report the procedure in the ELSO registry.

title: Coming Off ECMO Emergently
keywords: ECMO; EMERGENTLY; COMING OFF; COMING OFF ECMO EMERGENTLY; TROUBLESHOOTING; MANAGEMENT; ECMO MANAGEMENT

items.label: You suspect the need for coming off emergently
Call for help
Alert and/or activate the ECLS and the ICU teams
Identify the need for coming off emergently
If at least one of the following is true:
Massive air entrance
Refer to Air in Circuit
Accidental decannulation
Go to Accidental Decannulation
Acute circuit thrombosis
Go to No Flow
Major circuit disruption
Go to Air in Circuit
And if weaning is deemed feasible OR no other management option is feasible for any reason, proceed to Coming Off ECMO—Cannulas.
Coming Off ECMO—Cannulas
Coming off Emergently:
Clamp the return tubing to interrupt blood flow
Reduce RPM and SGF to 0
Clamp the drainage tubing
If the cannulas are not functional or no longer required:
Proceed to decannulation
Consider surgical repair or hemostatic devices for arterial cannulas
Use mattress suture in the skin for venous cannulas. Compression is not necessary unless there is formation.
If cutdown with ligation into the vessel, it will need surgical decannulation.
If one or more cannulas are still functional or required (also to be used as introducers for alternative cannula)
If coming off due to temporary loss of vascular access due to accidental decannulation, rupture or thrombosis of one cannula, consider:
Clamp the cannula(s) that are still required
Separate the circuit from the cannulas
Flush and clamp the cannulas which are still required
Proceed to Coming Off ECMO—Circuit.
Coming Off ECMO—Circuit
If the circuit is still required:
AND/OR
If the need for coming off is due to temporary loss of vascular access as a result of accidental decannulation, rupture or thrombosis of one cannula, in a scenario of resources constraint:
Keep the circuit functional by recirculating over a bridge OR keep the circuit functional by connecting drainage and return tubing to create a loop.
Flush and clamp the cannula still on site.
If the circuit is NOT functional OR no longer required:
Dispose of the circuit and the cannulas according to hospital protocol.
Clean the ECMO machine according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Proceed to Post-Coming Off Management.
Post-Coming Off and Ongoing Management
Optimize conventional respiratory and/or circulatory support as needed.
Consider post-decannulation screening of the cannulated vessels for complications and treat accordingly.
Consider surgical repair if the arterial vessel is involved.
If decannulation was associated with prolonged cardiac arrest, implement post-resuscitation care and implement as per guidelines.
Strictly monitor the patient.
Document the procedure in the patient's chart and include the reason for coming off and timing off.
Report the procedure in the ELSO registry.

title: Conversion of ECMO to CPB and Back Again
content: This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.
keywords: CONVERSION; CPB; ECMO; PROCEDURE

items.label: Conversion of ECMO to CPB and Back Again
Cool patient to 32℃ while opening the chest on ECMO.
Give 3mg/kg Heparin and allow it to circulate.
Check ACT >500 sec.
Clamp the ECMO circuit and connect the CPB circuit to the ECMO cannulas, or additional cannulas if necessary.
Go on CPB.
Connect the ends of the ECMO circuit together and recirculate.
Turn the sweep off.
Flash sweep for a few seconds if blood becomes deoxygenated.
Check ACT and blood gas periodically.
Give additional heparin if ACT drops below 500 seconds.
Perform the surgery.
If the patient will not come off CPB, reconnect to the same ECMO circuit if it’s clean.
If it was due to be changed, prime a new one.
Partially reverse heparin using ⅓ doses of Protamine (typically 1mg/kg).
Draw an ACT. Two to three minutes after each protamine dose, give an additional dose every time ACT exceeds 250 seconds.
Once ACT is less than 250 seconds, stop giving protamine. Give Platelets, FFP, Cryoprecipitate and PCC concurrently.
Red Cell salvage the CPB circuit.
If the patient does come off CPB, their passivated ECMO circuit can be kept on standby for 4–6 hours.

title: Coming Off ECMO
content: Use this checklist to guide the determination of death in patients on ECMO. These checklists may be adapted as necessary to meet local legal, regulatory, and/or institutional policy. Consider a low threshold for additional imaging to demonstrate the absence of cerebral blood flow.
keywords: Diagnose; Death; Neurological; Circulatory

items.label: Neurological Criteria for Determination of Death for Adults
Ensure that the patient has a systolic blood pressure ≥ 90-100 mmHg.
OR, if there is no/low pulsatility, use a mean arterial pressure ≥ 60 mmHg
Increase inotropes or extracorporeal blood flow as needed.
Ensure that the patient’s core temperature is ≥ 36C°.
Optimize the Heater Unit and/or Heater-Cooler Unit temperature as needed.
Ensure acid-base, metabolic, and endocrine homeostasis.
If not feasible, consider performing an ancillary test.
Possible ancillary tests include:
Cerebral angiography
Cerebral angio-CT
Transcranial doppler (TCD) adapted to to the age of the patient and to ECMO configuration
Exclude the influence of anesthetics, sedatives and neuromuscular blocking agents.
If needed, consider measuring plasmatic or urinary concentrations.
If highly lipophilic/protein bound medications have been used AND circuit sequestration cannot be excluded, consider increasing the length of the therapeutic window.
Visit Medications for additional information

Before performing the apnea test, maximize oxygenation both through mechanical ventilation and extracorporeal support, increasing both fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) and fraction of oxygen in the sweep gas flow (FsO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) to 100%.
Decrease sweep gas flow using a stepwise approach titrated on end-tidal CO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> to a minimum of 500/1000 mL (for adults).
Maintain extracorporeal blood flow.
Maintain continuous airway pressure to avoid derecruitment, particularly if the patient is a  potential lung donor.
Observe the patient for evidence of breaths. If the patient is breathing, abort the test immediately.
If hemodynamic instability occurs during the apnea test on VA ECMO, consider increasing the extracorporeal blood flow.
If severe desaturation occurs during the apnea test, temporarily increase SGF/FsO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> before repeating the test.
If instability persists during the apnea test (e.g., SpO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> < 85%, unstable arrhythmia/hypotension) consider an alternative test.
If the patient is stable, assess blood gas analysis to verify that the apnea test has been completed successfully.
Adapt sampling site(s) to ECMO configuration (e.g., if > 1 sample, all should be consistent with pH/PaCO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> requirements).
On VV ECMO, take the sample on the patient using standard practice.
On VA with no native cardiac function, take the sample on the circuit after the membrane lung (ML).
On VA or V-AV ECMO) with no native cardiac function, take the sample simultaneously from the patient at the right upper limb arterial site and on the circuit after the ML.
If the patient is a potential organ donor after the apnea test:
Resume baseline settings for mechanical ventilation and ECLS to optimize end-organ oxygen delivery.
If the patient is not considered for organ donation after declaration of death:
Interrupt ECLS clamping drainage and return limbs, interrupting SGF and stopping the ECLS pump.
Circulatory Criteria for Determination of Death
Clamp drainage and return lines.
Stop the ECMO pump and set sweep gas flow to zero.
If the patient is a potential organ donor and normothermic regional perfusion is a possibility, consider these prior to withdrawal of life saving measures.
Insert an A-V bridge allowing for recirculation into the ECMO circuit, allowing for the circuit to be used after determination of death.
Flush the cannulas to ensure patency.
Wait for asystole and assess for lack of spontaneous recovery of cardiac activity as required by local regulation and institutional policy.
If the patient is a potential organ donor and normothermic regional perfusion will be performed:
Implement a strategy to regionalize extracorporeal blood flow according to the mode of ECMO.
If in VA configuration: restart ECLS.
If in V-AV configuration: restart ECLS in VA configuration, keeping venous return line clamped.
If in VV configuration:
Insert an arterial cannula.
Disconnect the return line of the circuit.
Connect the return line to the arterial cannula and restart ECLS in VA configuration, keeping the venous return cannula clamped.
Suggested Readings

Neurological monitoring and management for adult extracorporeal membrane oxygenation patients: Extracorporeal Life Support Organization consensus guidelines [published correction appears in Crit Care. 2024 Oct 7;28(1):327. doi: 10.1186/s13054-024-05107-7.]. title: Switch from CPB to VA ECMO
content: Use this checklist when you need to switch from Cardiopulmonary Bypass (CPB) to VA ECMO. This is designed to initiate postcardiotomy ECMO in a patient that cannot wean from cardiopulmonary bypass after a cardiothoracic intervention.
keywords: CPB;  ECMO; Procedure; Central CPB; Peripheral CPB; Central VA ECMO; Peripheral VA ECMO; VA ECMO; switch; switch mode

items.label: Switching from central CPB to central VA ECMO OR from peripheral CPB to peripheral VA ECMO
Identify the roles and responsibilities with ECLS team members.
Bring the ECMO system and circuit of choice to the operating room.
Assemble and prime the ECMO system of choice.
OR
Use the first expiring pre-assembled and/or primed circuit available (according to Institution protocol).
Connect the ECMO gas blender to the gas source.
Connect the ECMO membrane lung (ML) to the Heater unit/Heater-Cooler unit and normalize the temperature according to the patient's needs.
Prepare the required straight connectors for drainage and return line, according to cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) and ECMO circuit tubing sizes.
Possible configuration for the adults, small adults, and older (larger) children:
½ - ⅜  connector for venous line if a ½ venous line was used during the CPB.
⅜ - ⅜ connector for venous line if a ⅜ venous line was used during.
⅜ - ⅜ connector for arterial line.
Possible configuration for pediatric patients:
⅜ - ¼ connector for venous line if a ⅜ venous line was used during the CPB.
¼ - ¼ connector for arterial line.
Possible configuration for infants:
¼ - ¼ connectors for venous and arterial lines.
Possible configuration for neonates:
¼ - ¼ connector for venous line.
3/16 - ¼ connector for arterial line.
Consider pre-oxygenating the patient increasing FsO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> to 100% to compensate for the temporary pump stop.
Place the sterile portion of the ECMO lines in the sterile field keeping two clamps on the non-sterile portions.
Clamp the drainage/return ECMO lines where required according to desired tubing length and cut as needed.
Insert the required straight connectors on the drainage/return ECMO lines.
The lead surgeon asks the perfusionist for a CPB pump STOP.
The perfusionist stops the CPB pump and verbally confirms.
Clamp the venous and arterial CPB lines close to the cannula.
Place another clamp at 10-15 cm and cut between the two clamps.
Connect the drainage/return ECMO lines using an air-free technique.
Verify that no air is present.
Unclamp the ECMO lines and ask the perfusionist to START the ECMO pump.
Remove the clamp on the ECMO drainage line, start the ECMO pump and when safe, remove the clamp on the return side and Confirm ECMO ON.
Restart the Sweep Gas Flow.
Verify that the target extracorporeal blood flow (EBF) is achieved.
Adjust the ECMO gas blender settings as necessary.
Adjust the Heater Unit/Heater-Cooler Unit water temperature as necessary.
Consider processing the blood inside the CPB circuit through a cell saver device to conserve blood loss.
DO NOT reverse anticoagulation.
Carefully monitor ACT without administering an additional dose until in range for ECMO (according to Institutional protocol).
Switch to the anticoagulation management/monitoring strategy adapted to the patient's characteristics and according to Institutional protocol.
Dress the insertion sites and adjust the tubing to meet the desired configuration.
When ready, move the patient to the ICU or desired location.

Select the cannulae according to the patient's characteristics, expected insertion sites, and target extracorporeal blood flow (EBF). Refer to the Cannulas for additional information and specifications.
Refer to Cannulas

Insert the drainage and return cannulas.

Carefully remove CPB cannulas and repair the insertion sites as needed.

Carefully monitor ACT without administering an additional dose until within range for ECMO (according to Institutional protocol).

title: Switch from VA ECMO to CPB
content: Use this checklist when you need to switch from VA ECMO to Cardiopulmonary Bypass (CPB). This procedure is required to initiate a cardiothoracic intervention requiring conventional CPB in a patient on VA ECMO.
keywords: CPB; ECMO; Procedure; Central CPB; Peripheral CPB; Central VA ECMO; Peripheral VA ECMO; VA ECMO; switch; switch mode

Identify the roles and responsibilities with ECLS team members.
Bring a CPB system and circuit of choice to the operating room.
Assemble and prime the CPB system of choice
OR

Prepare the ECMO cannulas and the distal portion of the ECMO tubings to be introduced to the sterile field, providing antiseptic solution to the incision area and cannulas/tubings (according to Institution protocol).

Continue the ACT monitoring and anticoagulation management strategy according to the Institution protocol for CPB throughout the procedure.
Once ACT > 400", the leading surgeon will typically ask the perfusionist to STOP the ECMO pump.
The perfusionist stops the ECMO pump and verbally confirms.
Place clamps on the drainage and return ECMO lines close to the cannulas. Put another clamp on both sides at 10/15 cm and cut between the two clamps.
Connect the drainage/return ECMO lines using an air-free technique.
Verify that no air is present in the circuit.
Unclamp the CPB lines and ask the perfusionist to START the CPB pump.
The perfusionist removes the clamp on the CPB drainage line, starts the CPB centrifugal pump and when safe, removes the clamp on return side and confirms ON BYPASS.
OR
Remove the clamp on the return side and start the CPB roller pump, release the clamp on the drainage line and confirm ON BYPASS.
Restart the sweep gas flow.
Verify that the target extracorporeal blood flow is achieved.
Adjust the CPB gas blender settings as necessary.
Adjust the HCU water temperature as necessary to reach target temperature according to the patient and the procedure.
Consider processing the blood inside the CPB circuit through a cell saver device to conserve blood loss.
Consider connecting the drainage and return line of the CPB circuit through a straight connector to create a loop.
Keep the ECMO circuit running to be used at the end of CPB, if possible and desired.
If the circuit is retained, reduce the sweep gas flow to 0 and disconnect the gas line from the ML gas inlet.
At the end of the procedure, if is ECMO still required:
Gradually start ECMO flow and sweep gas flow.
Gradually wean from CPB to provide consistent expected oxygen delivery throughout the procedure.
Verify that the target extracorporeal blood flow is achieved.
Adjust the ECMO gas blender settings as necessary.
Adjust the Heater Unit/Heater-Cooler Unit water temperature as necessary.
Once able to provide full ECMO extracorporeal blood flow, clamp the CPB lines and stop the pump.
Carefully remove the CPB cannulas and repair the insertion sites as needed.
Consider processing the blood inside the CPB circuit through a cell saver device to conserve blood loss.
DO NOT reverse anticoagulation.
Carefully monitor ACT without administering an additional dose until in range for ECMO (according to Institutional protocol).
Switch to the anticoagulation management/monitoring strategy adapted to patient's characteristics (according to Institutional protocol).
Dress the insertion sites and adjust the tubing according to the desired configuration.
Once ready, move the patient to the ICU or alternative location, as required.
At the end of the procedure, if ECMO is NOT required:
Wean from CPB.
Proceed with anticoagulation reversal, according to Institutional protocol.
Remove the CPB cannulas, repairing insertion points as needed.
Consider processing the blood inside the CPB and ECMO circuit through a cell saver device to conserve blood loss.

Possible configuration for the adult/small adult/older (larger) children:

Unclamp and restart the pump.
Confirm ECMO ON and confirm flow.
Confirm no excessive PA pressure rise after flow initiation.
Confirm final PA cannula position.
Exclude PA injury hazards after placement:
PA rupture / pulmonary hemorrhage
Tricuspid or pulmonary valve injury
New arrhythmia
New pericardial effusion
Acute hemodynamic deterioration
DO NOT advance the cannula against resistance.
Switch to VA + LV Unloading — Workflow
Identify the roles and responsibilities with ECMO team members.
Assess aortic valve opening, LV size/distension on echo, pulmonary edema, pulse pressure, PCWP/LA pressure if available.
Select unloading option:
Mechanical unloading
Atrial-level unloading
Surgical vent
Confirm compatibility with current configuration.
Confirm escalation pathway if first option fails (according to institutional protocol).
Bring required equipment to the bedside.
Deploy unloading option per plan.
Reassess LV size and aortic valve opening after deployment.
Reassess pulmonary edema and pulse pressure.
Escalate immediately if LV overload is severe or worsening.
Reassess Immediately After Switch
Target EBF achieved.
Flow distribution at planned split if VVA.
MAP and systemic perfusion at patient target.
Oxygenation at patient target (right-radial SpO₂ if VA or VVA).
CO₂ clearance at target.
Lactate, CVP, PA pressure (if PA cannula), LV loading (if VA component) reassessed.
Distal limb perfusion intact if femoral arterial return.
Final cannula position reconfirmed.
Termination: Target Configuration Achieved
Maintain target EBF and flow distribution.
Label all drainage and return limbs.
Document final configuration, cannula type / size / depth / access site, and flow split if VVA.
Define monitoring priorities by configuration and reassessment time.
Communicate plan to ICU, procedural, perfusion, and bedside teams.
Termination: Target Configuration NOT Achieved
Call senior ECMO, procedural, surgical, and perfusion support if unsafe or ineffective.
Wrong target configuration? Reassess physiology matrix.
Cannula malposition? Image and reposition. Refer to Cannula Exit Sites and Tubings Management.
Insufficient drainage or excessive negative drainage pressure? Check volume, position, and additional drainage. Refer to Manage Drainage Insufficiency on ECMO.
High return pressure? Check cannula size, oxygenator, and for kinks. Refer to Membrane Lung Failure
Pump or oxygenator flow limitation? Assess the circuit and consider component change.
Excessive recirculation? Reposition or change drainage strategy. Refer to Identification and management of recirculation in venovenous ECMO for more information.
Persistent differential oxygenation? Revisit flow split or upper-body return.
LV overload? Escalate LV unloading pathway.
PA/RV injury (rupture, hemorrhage, valve injury, arrhythmia, effusion)? Echo and surgical consult.
Bleeding/hypovolemia? Perform product replacement and surgical control as required.
Hemolysis?vAssess pump and oxygenator. Consider component change.
Low-flow limb thrombosis? Perform DPC review and anticoagulation review.
DO NOT persist with a failed configuration without senior review.
With Any Termination
Inform family/surrogates.
Report event in detail.
Update local and ELSO Registry documentation.
Update cannula and circuit labels.

items.label: Prior to Transport
Identify the need for transport
Is the patient appropriate to transport?
Is it the right time for transport?
Is the appropriate transport team available?
Assign a transport team leader.
Allocate roles to staff members on transport team according to appropriate skill set:
Composition of the team would depend on individual country/ institution requirements and case complexity. The team should be capable of managing ECMO emergencies and providing resuscitation.
Common members on a transport team include ECMO surgeon or physician, ECMO specialist, perfusionist, critical care nurse and respiratory therapist.
All members should be familiar with the patient, equipment and medications used during transport.
Communication:
Team leader(s) should inform transport team members about the details of the transport arrangements, including location, any infectious disease status and precautionary measures.
Notify the receiving destination team and provide them with adequate information, including the estimated arrival time.
Plan the best route, secure the lift and clear the passageway beforehand.
Do not initiate the transport until the destination site has made all necessary preparations to receive the patient.
Inform the patient and the family.
Prepare the equipment used for transport:
Transport stretcher
Emergency transport equipment
Non-emergency transport equipment
Intra-hospital transportation bag (See Appendix B)
Prepare ECMO for transport:
Check battery status of the ECMO console.
Check the settings and alarm limits in the pump console in use.
Secure all cannulas and circuit tubing.
Check that all connections are tightened.
Assess the risk, benefit and feasibility of transporting the patient with the ECMO console alone or with the ECMO cart.
Assess whether water lines and circuit pressure monitoring lines can be temporarily disconnected during transport.
Bring strong ECMO clamps, hand crank or spare ECMO console (depending on machine used).
Immediately before transport:
The team leader should optimally stabilize and re-assess the patient.
Check ECMO settings and ECMO parameters.
Connect the ECMO console to UPS, if appropriate.
Bring an adequate gas cylinder (oxygen cylinder of adequate volume for the journey, with or without a compressed air cylinder depending on the transport set-up).

Check non-ECMO transport equipment and ECMO equipment including ECMO circuit after disconnection of power supplies and connection of gas supply to transport gas cylinder(s) / compressor. Refer to Mobile ECMO.
Set appropriate alarm settings for non-ECMO and ECMO equipment.
Securely mount or strap all ECMO and non-ECMO equipment on the appropriate platform against vibration and potential impact.
Allow for ready access to hand crank or backup pump, so that flow can be re-established promptly in the event of in transit console failure.
Secure the oxygenator at a level below the patient during ECMO support.
During Transport or After Arrival to Destination
Continuously monitor and regularly document the patient's condition and ECMO parameters.
After arrival to the destination and re-establishing power and gas supplies, check non-ECMO transport equipment and ECMO equipment including ECMO circuit. (See Appendix A)
Check ECMO settings and ECMO parameters.
If the ECMO transport team needs to leave the patient, the team leader must re-assess the patient's condition and properly hand over the patient to the appropriate receiving team.
Before Leaving the Destination
Secure patient and all equipment on the transport stretcher.
Check ECMO settings and ECMO parameters.

Check non-ECMO transport equipment and ECMO equipment including ECMO circuit after disconnection of power supplies and connection of gas supply to transport gas cylinder(s)/ compressor. Refer to Mobile ECMO.
After Transport
After returning to the parent unit and re-establishing power and gas supplies, check non-ECMO transport equipment and ECMO equipment including ECMO circuit. (See Appendix A)
Check ECMO settings and ECMO parameters.
Team leader should re-assess the patient and declare completion of the transport mission when all therapies are resumed.

Gas supply (including proper connection of the gas lines, proper functioning of all gas supply equipment (e.g., air-oxygen blender) and adequacy of gas supply for the journey).

title: Manage Drainage Insufficiency on ECMO
content:
Pre-pump failure to deliver venous blood at the required rate.
Signs: Chatter/chugging, swings in Pven, flow that won't rise with RPM.
Trigger intervention on circuit signs: By the time hypoxia (VV) or hypotension (VA) appears, hemolysis and microemboli have already occurred. Approach is similar for VA and VV; specifics noted below.

This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.
keywords: VV ECMO; VA ECMO; DRAINAGE INSUFFICIENCY; MANAGEMENT; ECMO

items.label: Recognition: Identify the event
Any one of the following options:
chatter/chugging
flow below target
flow that won't rise with RPM
sustained or swinging Pven,
drainage line color change.
Confirm pre-pump (not post-pump, not pump-related).
Consider iatrogenic over-speed first:
Is oxygen delivery adequate (capillary refill, mentation, urine output, lactate)?
Was RPM recently increased?
Was the patient recently diurested, repositioned, or extubated?
Stabilize: Reduce pump speed until flow is stable and chatter resolves
Step down by 5–10% of set RPM (~100–200 RPM in adults) until chatter resolves and flow stabilizes.
Do not chase flow with RPM. If a higher RPM no longer produces higher flow, you are above drainage capacity.
Hold at the lowest stable speed that supports the patient.
Note: Excessively negative drainage pressure causes vessel collapse, cavitation, hemolysis, and microemboli. Operator-set over-speed is the single most common cause.
Triage: Characterize the drainage signal
Chatter resolves with speed reduction
Preload supply problem
Persistent chatter or sustained high negative Pven
Partial cannula obstruction ± preload supply
Low flutter, no chatter, flat Pven
Fixed mechanical obstruction OR profound hypovolemia.
VV stable flow and Pven but falling SpO<sub>2</sub>
Demand problem, not drainage
Note: Mixed pictures are common. When in doubt, run pathways in parallel.
Preload-Supply Pathway: Address reversible causes
Position
Mild head-down tilt (5–10°) as a free diagnostic-therapeutic test; resolution within seconds suggests volume responsiveness.
Warning: Avoid head-down tilt in raised ICP, recent neurosurgery, severe pulmonary edema, or severe ARDS.
Agitation/Valsalva
Confirm adequate sedation first; add NMB only if dyssynchrony persists.
Intrathoracic/intra-abdominal pressure
Rule out tension PTX, tamponade, auto-PEEP, IAH (POCUS, bladder pressure).
Cannula position
Femoral tip in mid-to-high IVC at/just below cavoatrial junction (avoid deep RA).
Confirm by POCUS/echo
Reposition only under imaging.
Bleeding
Treat source.
Consider anticoagulation reversal effects on low transmembrane blood flow.
Transfuse to physiologic Hb target—this is replacement, distinct from crystalloid loading.
Vasodilation
Vasopressor to venoconstrict and maintain MAP target
Crystalloid only if step 4 confirms response.
Preload-Supply Pathway: Test Crystalloid Responsiveness
Addressing the reversible causes is insufficient.
250 mL crystalloid challenge while monitoring flow, Pven, MAP, chatter.
If responsive—e.g., flow rises, Pven normalizes, chatter resolves—resuscitate to euvolemia (adequate oxygen delivery – capillary refill, mentation, urine output, lactate), then STOP.
If non-responsive, no further crystalloid.
Note: Positive crystalloid balance is associated with prolonged ECMO duration and higher mortality.
Mechanical Pathway: Inspect and Image (Bedside, immediate)
Trace the circuit patient-to-pump. Look for kinks, clamps, dressing compression, line tangle, visible clot, and/or color changes at hub/line/inlet.
Compare the flow at two RPM settings. A minimal rise with disproportionate Pven fall is a fixed obstruction.
Ultrasound the accessible cannula course for intraluminal echogenic material; echo/TEE for tip patency.
Send free Hb, LDH, fibrinogen, D-dimer, platelets for trend. Do not wait for results to act.
Reassess and Escalate: Interventions
If two interventions don't help, return to Recognition: Identify the event
The working diagnosis may be wrong (demand-driven, return-side, tamponade missed)
Reassess and Escalate: Escalation Triggers
Inadequate flow with compromise persisting >5–10 min despite steps 1–5.
Rising free Hb (commonly >50 mg/dL or doubling from baseline).
Visible/audible cavitation or microemboli
Oxygen delivery, SpO₂ or MAP drop below local threshold attributable to the event.
Reassess and Escalate: Escalation Options
Add second drainage cannula (contralateral femoral or jugular)—often lowest-risk; existing cannula remains as fallback.
Reposition existing cannula under imaging—only if malposition is clearly identified.
Exchange cannula/circuit—for confirmed thrombosis.
Reconfigure (VV → VVA)—only for mixed cardiac/respiratory failure.
This is a major undertaking, not routine.
Reassess and Escalate: If Resources Exceeded
Call regional ECMO center early; maintain lowest stable RPM
VA ECMO Additions: Native Cardiac Recovery Competing for Preload
Recovering heart captures venous return — sign of recovery, not a problem to solve with RPM.
Titrate the flow down to match if anticoagulation adequate; plan trial-off when hemodynamics, lactate, and echo support.
VV ECMO Additions: Demand-driven vs. Supply-limited
Stable circuit but falling SpO<sub>2</sub> is a demand problem. Do not give fluid.
Treat fever, deepen sedation, treat sepsis, reduce work of breathing.
VV ECMO Additions: Recirculation
Clues:
Bright drainage blood
Disproportionately high pre-membrane SvO₂
Paradoxical desaturation at higher RPM
Narrow AV gap.
SvO₂ alone is unreliable (septic high-output patients can have genuinely high SvO₂). Use calculation methods (Walker, Lindholm) where available.
Causes:
Tip migration
Small RA
Low CO
Excessive ECMO flow.
Address cause
Reposition or reduce flow as indicated
Prevention
Large-bore drainage cannulae (25–29 Fr adult, vessel permitting); multistage where available.
Femoral tip high IVC; proximal holes above iliac bifurcation.
Titrate to patient need, not maximum flow. Lowest speed that meets demand.
Maintain minimum flow to avoid clotting during recovery.
Document per-patient baseline (Pven at set RPM, flow, line behavior) at initiation.
Resource-Limited Settings
No transducers
rely on flow, chatter, line inspection
Document baseline.
No POCUS
CXR for cannula position
Clinical exam for tamponade/PTX/IAH
Slow labs
Treat clinical hemolysis (pink plasma, rising bilirubin, Hb drop without bleeding) as the threshold
No backup
Call referral center early; do not manipulate cannulae without backup.
Roles During the Event
Leader:
Runs algorithm
Prioritizes sequence of examination and interventions
Calls for help
Bedside RN:
Vitals
Medications
Fluid/transfusion
Patient-side changes
Perfusionist/ECMO specialist
Circuit management and inspection.
Sonographer/Second Operator:
POCUS/echo on request
Respiratory therapist/Physician:
Mechanical ventilator changes.
Closed-loop communication on every RPM change and drug.
If two interventions worsen the situation, stop and reassess from Recognition: Identify the Event.

title: VA ECMO
content: Use this checklist to manage gas exchange in patients on VA ECMO configurations.
keywords: Gas; Exchange; Configurations;

items.label: Oxygenation
Stabilize the patient (6-12 hours).

Assess oxygen delivery/oxygen consumption (VO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) ≥ 3:1, mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) ≥65-70% and oxygen saturation of arterial blood (SaO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) around 90%.
If NO, increase blood flow and optimize hemoglobin (Hb) to 12-14 g/dL.
If YES, continue to the next step.
Achieve pulse pressure ≥10-15 mmHg.
If NO (non-pulsatile flow), unload the left ventricle (LV) by decreasing blood flow.
If YES, continue to the next step.

Note: when the heart begins to recover—increased pulse pressure and decreased blood flow—titrate down the flow to maintain a venous saturation of >70%. When the heart function is adequate, conduct a trial off bypass.
Titrate fraction of delivered oxygen (FsO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>), which is the fraction of O<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> in the SGF.
Target slight hypoxemia (PaO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> ~150 mmHg) after the membrane lung.
Arterial return saturation (S<sub class="math-sub">post</sub>O<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) should be close to 100%.
PO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> in arterial return (P<sub class="math-sub">post</sub>O<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) should be >2-5 times the FsO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>.
Manage the patient based on continuous venous and arterial saturation monitoring. Calculate the variables if oxygen supply seems excessive or inadequate.
Carbon dioxide (CO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) removal
For adults, set sweep gas flow (SGF) between ~50-100% of the ECMO blood flow, but not less than 500 mL.
For neonates and pediatrics, set SGF between ~50-100% of the ECMO blood flow.
For patients of all ages, check blood gas analysis within five minutes to prevent hypocapnia.
Adjust ventilator rest settings.
Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) and fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) to achieve an adequate PaO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> in the right arm.
Avoid hyperoxemia.
If there is heart and lung participation, adjust the ventilatory settings to regulate partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) (within lung protection).
Measure partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) at the right upper limb and post-membrane lung if the heart is ejecting.
If ~35-45 mmH<sub class="math-sub">2</sub>O, continue
If <35 mmH<sub class="math-sub">2</sub>O, decrease (↓) sweep flow
If >45 mmH<sub class="math-sub">2</sub>O, increase (↑) sweep flow
Note: If PCO2 ≥ 80-90 mmH2O, avoid abruptly dropping the PCO2 (which is associated with neurological injury). Hypercapnia may be gradually controlled.

title: VV ECMO
content: Use this checklist to manage gas exchange in patients on VV ECMO configurations.
keywords: Gas; Exchange; Configurations;

items.label: Oxygenation
If the native lung is not working, set the ECMO flow to 60-80% of the measured cardiac output:
Stabilize the patient (6-12 hours).
Assess DO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>/VO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> >3:1, SaO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> >85-90%.
If YES, no changes are necessary.
If NO, optimize hemoglobin (Hb) to between 12-14 g/dL.
Note: There is a tradeoff of risk between transfusion and increasing circuit flow which favors transfusion of red blood cells (RBCs). Membrane lungs function optimally at a normal hematocrit.
If delivered oxygen (DO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>) is still inadequate, change the drainage cannula to a larger size (or adding additional venous drainage access) and increase blood flow.
Avoid hypoxemia (PaO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> < 60 mmHg).
Improvement in lung function?
If YES, continue to next step.

Note: As soon as there is lung recovery (defined as increased DO2 by the native lung and a decreased need for a DO2 by the ECMO circuit) requiring less blood flow or allowing a lower level of hemoglobin, start VV ECMO weaning.

If NO, consider high O<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> consumption (fever, sepsis, activity) or recirculation (high SvO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub> and SaO<sub class="math-sub mr-pad">2</sub>).
Note: If recirculation is suspected:
Refer to the Recirculation calculator
Check the distance between the drainage and return cannulas (>8-10 cm, 15 is better)
If DLC, check its position
Look for tension PTX, cardiac tamponade or other cause impairing venous return
Verify that EBF is not excessive in relation to cannula size

title: Neuromonitoring on ECMO
content: This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.
keywords: NEUROMONITORING; ECMO MANAGEMENT; TRANSCRANIAL DOPPLER; CONTINUOUS EEG; NIRS; CEREBRAL OXIMETRY; HEAD CT; CRANIAL ULTRASOUND; CUS; NEUROLOGIC INJURY

items.label: Background
Wide range of short and long-term disabilities including motor impairment and cognitive delays, behavioral abnormalities, and lower quality of life scores compared to healthy and non-ECMO patients.
There is currently no consensus about the most reliable and effective way to provide neuromonitoring care for patients on ECMO.
Not all modalities are widely available.
Many studies looking at neuromonitoring are largely based on single center experience.
Many of these modalities determine injury after it has already occurred and do not in and of themselves predict neurologic risk.
ELSO has put out a neuromonitoring guideline for pediatric and neonatal patients based on expert consensus.

Neuromonitoring in Neonates and Children Undergoing ECMO
RECOMMENDED
HUS
HUS should be obtained pre- and post-ECMO initiation, and considered daily for three to five days if initial HUS is abnormal or in high-risk infants with open fontanelle. HUS should be performed as needed if clinical indication, followed by series of HUS as required.
Continuous EEG
cEEG monitoring can be considered within 12–24 hours after ECMO cannulation for at least 24–48 hours. Consider prolonged cEEG, (at least 24 hours) if seizures/interictal abnormalities detected (intermittent EEG in resource limited settings).
Cerebral rSO2
Consider continuous rSO2 monitoring (frontal probes) in all patients on ECMO to follow trends in cerebral tissue oxygenation. A decline >20% from baseline can be associated with injury and may warrant further workup.
Head CT
Head CT should be obtained in infants and children on ECMO if there is a clinical concern of an acute neurological insult or if abnormal findings are noticed on other neuromonitoring modalities, such as head ultrasound or cerebral oximetry.
OPTIONAL
SSEP
Evidence on role of Somatosensory Evoked Potential to detect neurological injuries is limited in patients on ECMO support and is not recommended for routine neuro monitoring.
TCD
Cerebral Blood Flow Velocities (CBFV) and pulsatility index (PI) measurement through TCD ultrasound may detect neurological injuries, but, to date, evidence on ECMO patients is limited, and is not recommended for routine monitoring.
Brain Injury Biomarkers
Plasma brain injury markers are under investigation to detect neurological injuries on ECMO, but currently are not rapidly available, and are not recommended for routine monitoring.
Pupillometry
Pupillometry may help with early neuroprognostication, however limited studies are available, and is not recommended for routine monitoring on ECMO.
High-risk groups for neurologic injury
Patient risk factors
Prematurity
Low body weight
Cardiac failure

High risk patient groups

Cannulation type/strategy
Cranial Ultrasound (CUS)
Population:
Patients with open fontanelle
Obtained prior to ECMO (when feasible)
Obtained after ECMO initiation everyday x 3–5 days in infants with abnormal CUS and high-risk infants with open fontanelle.
Benefits:
Easy to do at bedside/portable
No radiation
Caveats:
Utility based on skill of ultrasonographer
If abnormal CUS, consider head CT (CUS has low specificity for hemorrhage/ischemic changes, may miss bleeds in certain areas of the brain)
Head CT
Population:
Patients with cardiac arrest or ECPR (obtain within 24 hours if clinically feasible)
Acute change in neurologic status, mental status, pupillary changes, seizures, focal neurologic deficit, or weakness
Change from baseline in other monitoring (i.e. change in NIRS, change on CUS, seizures on EEG)
Portable head CT when possible—sufficient sensitivity to detect many neurologic insults
Large body habitus may limit the ability to perform (check with radiology tech for measurements if concerned)
If unable to obtain portable and patient is stable on ECMO, see transport section
Benefits:
23–32% of patients getting head CT will require intervention (change in management, neurosurgical intervention, withdrawal of care)
Continuous EEG
Population:
Seizures noted in between 18-23% of neonatal and pediatric ECMO patients with ~50-80% of those seizures being subclinical
Consider EEG in all ECMO patients for the first 48 hours with initiation 12–24 hours post cannulation.
Can consider early discontinuation in patients who are awake and neurologically appropriate
Most seizures are detected in the first 24 hours of EEG monitoring with ¾ of seizures detected within first 72 hours in one study
If seizures present continue EEG for at least 24 hours post seizure control
Poor background reactivity and lack of variation have been associated with poor prognosis of ECMO patients
Limitations:
May be limited by epileptologist availability to read 24 hours, machine/technology availability
Cerebral Oximetry (NIRS- near-infrared spectroscopy)
Utilized to follow TRENDS in cerebral tissue oxygenation
A 20% decrease from baseline has been associated with neurologic injury and may warrant additional work-up
Population:
All ECMO patients
Okay to defer utilization while the EEG is in place, if it’s not feasible to place both due to available real estate
Okay to consider intermittent monitoring in awake, neurologically appropriate patients
Limitations:
Few studies with ECMO patients
May have changes in NIRS during variations in ECMO flow but not necessarily correlation with clinical change or neurologic injury
Transcranial Doppler
Measure of cerebral blood flow velocities and pulsatility index can detect neurologic injury
Can measure CBF velocity in anterior, middle and posterior cerebral circulation as well as internal carotid
CBF seems to be decreased in ECMO patients compared to controls (sick and healthy) and higher after decannulation
May be able to predict risk before it happens
Current Evidence
Limited to small studies
Focal elevations/asymmetries also associated with neurologic injuries 1–4 days prior to notation of injury
Benefits
Non-invasive, portable
Limitations
Operator dependent—must account for user variation during interpretation
May have limited center availability and experience for machine availability and radiologist interpretation
May have decreased ability to utilize this technology based on decreased cardiac function as there may be reduced cerebral pulsatility
Adjunct Technology—More Data Emerging
Pupillometry
Population: Adjunct technology; data supporting use of pupilometry in ECMO populations is currently limited
Consider utilization in populations where there is difficulty in determining pupil reactivity or asymmetry
May be a good prognosticator of mortality in certain ECMO populations however, more data is needed
MRI
Low-field portable MRI has been shown to be safe and feasible on patients on ECMO. However, this technology is currently not widely available.
Population: All patients prior to discharge
Ideally obtained 7–10 days post-insult leading to ECMO or neurologic insult on ECMO.

Reposition the electrocardiogram (EKG) leads to the patient's back.
Position the circuit tubing, lines, and drains above the waist towards the head of the bed, and those below the waist towards the foot of the bed.
Ensure the availability of emergency equipment and a crash cart at the bedside.

Organize an adequate number of trained staff for the position change (at least six staff members).
Discuss and confirm the roles of each member.
Assign one staff member to take care of the ECMO console and tubing.

Lower ECMO flow
Accidental extubation, decannulation, or line displacement
Bleeding from ECMO cannula sites
Machine malfunction

Turning an ECMO Patient
Complete this checklist if you are turning an ECMO patient from the prone position to a supine position.
Team members should always follow the team leader’s command.
Closely monitor the ECMO blood flow and line pressures during a position change.
Ensure patient safety during position change:
One staff member at the head end guides the procedure, and holds the artificial airway and the jugular ECMO cannula, if present.
One staff member at the feet end holds the ECMO cannula and tubing while monitoring ECMO parameters.
At least two staff members standing on each side of the bed to help turn the patient using the double-sheets technique.
Avoid placing any tension on the ECMO tubing during turning.
Monitor the patient’s physiological parameters for changes and tolerance to the prone position.
During Prone Positioning
Complete this checklist if the ECMO patient is in a prone position.
Continuously monitor the patient’s vitals and response to prone therapy.
Closely monitor the ECMO blood flow and line pressures for any adjustments that may be necessary.
Free breasts, abdomen, and genitals from any pressure.
For obese patients, position the abdomen carefully to avoid an increase in intra-abdominal pressure and use a reverse Trendelenburg position, if possible.
Reposition the patient's head and upper limbs at regular intervals according to institutional policy.
Protect body areas with dedicated pillows or pressure relieving devices to prevent pressure injuries.
Turning a Patient Back to Supine Position
Complete this checklist if you are turning an ECMO patient from the prone position to a supine position.
The procedure is a reversal of the prone positioning maneuver.
Use extreme caution to avoid accidental extubation, decannulation, and patient injuries.
Check the patients’ vitals to confirm stability. Intervene immediately if vitals become unstable.
Confirm that the cannula positions have remained unchanged.
Confirm that ECMO blood flow and line pressures are within target ranges.
Evaluate the patient’s response after turning them back to a supine position, and determine a plan for the next day if indicated.

title: UFH Anticoagulation Monitoring and Management
content:
This checklist outlines the monitoring and management of unfractionated heparin (UFH) anticoagulation in patients on ECMO.

Anticoagulation should be monitored in the context of their individual baseline (as opposed to a laboratory baseline), overall inflammatory state — such as septic shock, end-organ dysfunction (liver and kidney) and platelet function as well as consideration of their unique bleeding and clotting risks.

Variability and therapeutic ranges differ between clinical sites and should be individualized.
keywords: UFH; Unfractionated Heparin; Anticoagulation; Monitoring; Management; Algorithm

items.label: ECMO Cannulation
UFH IV Bolus: 50-100 IU/kg
Consider dose according to coagulation status and bleeding risk.
UFH Monitoring
Determine activated clotting time (ACT)
Suggested range for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO): 180-200 seconds.
If prolonged, consider hypothermia, platelet function/number, and coagulation factor levels.
Note: ACT with other coagulation tests (including anti-Xa/heparin levels and aPTT) is frequently discordant.
Determine activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
Suggested therapeutic targets: 40–50 seconds initially, then titrated to 60–80 seconds depending on bleeding and/or thrombosis risk.
This test does not account for platelet function or clot strength. It evaluates clot formation based on mechanical or optical clot detection with ellagic acid.
Lower targets in VV ECMO possible:

LowAntiXa: 0.2–0.3 IU/mL
aPTT: 40–55s (ratio 1.2–1.6)
ModerateAntiXa: 0.3–0.5 IU/mL
aPTT: 50–70s (ratio 1.5–2.0)
HighAntiXa: 0.5–0.7 IU/mL
aPTT: 60–80s (ratio 1.8–2.4)
Note: aPTT is affected by antithrombin, factor VIII, factor XII, and fibrinogen levels. There is often discordance with anti-Xa monitoring.
Determine anti-factor Xa levels
Suggested ECMO target levels range: 0.3-0.7 IU/mL.
This test correlates better with unfractionated heparin (UFH) levels than aPTT.

Note: Anti-factor Xa does not evaluate clot formation, and it can be influenced by patient AT deficiency, hyperlipidemia, coagulation factor hemolysis with increased plasma hemoglobin/or hyperbilirubinemia.
Evaluate viscoelastic tests (e.g., TEG and ROTEM)
ROTEM: rotational thromboelastometry
TEG: thromboelastometry

These tests incorporate platelet function and assess clot strength using specific activators (e.g., tissue factor, ellagic acid, kaolin) to evaluate whole blood clot formation, and are often used for bleeding management evaluation rather than anticoagulation monitoring.
Optimize antithrombin (AT)
This is critical for heparin effectiveness.
Levels decrease during ECMO due to consumptive coagulopathy and other causes.
Note: There is no data supporting improved outcomes with supplementation in ECMO patients.
For additional information, refer to the Discrepancy between aPTT and AntiXa with UFH table.
UFH Management
UFH bolus at cannulation for ECMO
ELSO recommends:
Adults and newborns 50–100 U/kg.
Adjust based on pre-existing bleeding disorders:
Postsurgical ECMO (especially postcardiotomy)
Recent trauma
Type of cannulation (surgical or arterial at increased risk)
ECMO duration
Pre-ECMO coagulation abnormalities
On-ECMO aPTT >72 s, fibrinogen <2 g/L, and platelets count <38,000/mm³
Continuous infusion dose
ELSO recommends:
Adults 7.5–20 U/kg/hr and newborns 20–50 U/kg/hr.
Adjust based on:
aPTT ratio (goal of 1.5-2.5)
Anti-Xa levels (goal: 0.3-0.7 U/mL)
ACT
Viscoelastic tests
Discrepant Anticoagulation Tests
Anti-Xa levels between 0.3–0.7 U/mL.
aPTT <60 s, consider a hypercoagulable state.
aPTT 60-90 s, no change.
aPTT >90 s, repeat aPTT, consider fresh frozen plasma (FFP) if still high.
Anti-Xa levels <0.3 U/mL.
aPTT <60 s, increase heparin.
aPTT 60-90 s, increase heparin.
aPTT >90 s, consider factor deficiency and repletion with FFP.
Anti-Xa levels >0.7 U/mL.
aPTT <60 s, unlikely to occur; consider repeat labs.
aPTT 60-90 s, consider repeat labs or a hypercoagulable state.
aPTT >90 s, decrease heparin.
If there is a discrepancy between anticoagulation tests, please refer to the Discrepancy between aPTT and AntiXa with UFH Table under Medications.
Common problems occurring during heparin use for ECMO therapy
High heparin dose to reach target? Or target not reached?
Consider heparin resistance (>35,000 units/day)
Determine antithrombin (AT) levels
Consider repletion (desirable range in adults: 80–120%, there is no established baseline AT levels in children)
Evaluate other causes such as hyperfibrinogenemia or thrombocytosis
If problem remains consider changing to DTI
Decreasing platelet count (~50% or progressive).
Evaluate for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) (determine PF4 antibodies)
If Platelet Factor 4 (PF4) antibodies are positive and clinically compatible with HIT, send functional assay and switch to direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI)
In case of DIC, consider clotting in circuit and circuit exchange
In thrombocytopenia < 50,000 due to patient related problems and after exclusion of HIT, consider platelet transfusion and/or reduced anticoagulation level
Thrombosis
If clotting of membrane lung: exchange
If there is repeated clotting and/or systemic thrombosis, consider increasing heparin and search for hypercoagulable state:
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
Antiphospholipid Ab
Major bleeding
This includes:
Intracranial hemorrhage
Surgical site bleeding
Gastrointestinal and pulmonary hemorrhage
Cannulation site bleeding
Reduce or stop heparin, and keep pump blood flow high.
Local hemostasis (wounds, cannula, GI, etc.) if possible.
Check for coagulation disorders and correct.
If anti-Xa levels are above target, reduce.
If factors II, V, VII, X deficiency, replete.
If platelet deficiency (excluding HIT), consider platelet transfusion.
If DIC and hyperfibrinolysis, treat the cause and consider membrane lung change.
If acquired Von Willebrand syndrome, repletion and reduce ECMO pump speed if possible.
Note: Case reports and case series have reported successful management of bleeding of patients with ECMO with prolonged periods of no anticoagulation.

content: This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.

items.label: Identify the need for whole circuit replacement
All three checks are required, otherwise do NOT proceed with the whole circuit replacement.
Note: We do NOT recommend the replacement of a functioning circuit (e.g., due date as per IFU), as the risks associated with replacement outweigh the benefits.
A dysfunctional circuit: (at least one check)
Circuit thrombosis (minor membrane lung (ML) clotting not severely impacting with its function excluded) or unexplained coagulopathy.
Refer to Membrane Lung Failure.
Pump thrombosis
Massive air entrance
Refer to Air in Circuit
ML/pumphead rupture (if a rupture of a minor component) selectively change or isolate
A positive culture from the circuit refractory to optimize treatment/sustained by MRD/EDR/PDR organisms AND/OR evidence of microorganism growth on the ML
No weaning potential
Selective replacement of the involved component is not feasible for any reason.
Go to Component Replacement checklist
Alert/activate the ECLS and the ICU teams and assign clear roles
1 experienced intensivist and/or 1 experienced ICU nurse to support the patient
2 ECMOlogists to simultaneously work on drainage/return as sterile operators lines if elective procedure
At least 1 ECMOlogists to work on drainage/return lines as sterile operator if emergent procedure (2 operators are better, if feasible)
At least 1 ECMO specialist/perfusionist to prepare and manage the new circuit
At least 1 supporting healthcare worker
If this is an elective procedure, consider a short briefing.
Prepare the Essential Equipment
Consider also keeping an ECMO cart close to the procedure for emergencies.
Refer to the ECMO Cart checklist for more information.
Consider reading Chapters 4 and 7 of the ELSO Red Book, 6th edition for air-free connection.
Go to ELSO Red Book, 6th edition
Sterile consumables for setting up a sterile field
Sterile tubing scissors
2 sterile tubing clamps for drainage line tubing clamps
1 sterile bowl
2 sterile tubing clamps for return line
2 back-up sterile clamps
