OR
Primed back-up circuit on a back-up pump
2 straight connectors adapted to circuit tubing size OR cannulas
Scalpel to remove the tubing from the connector
Disinfecting solution and/or applicators for tubing preparation (per center institutional policy)
Prepare the Patient
Consider all of the following:
Supine the patient as ready for initiation.
If the patient is awake, inform him/her and/or their surrogate about the need for replacement, the procedure and potential associated risks.
If the patient is awake, consider sedation if deemed necessary.
Improve mechanical ventilation settings as ready to interrupt EBF on VV ECMO, V-AV ECMO, VP ECMO.
Improve inotropic/vasopressor support as ready to interrupt EBF on VA ECMO, V-AV ECMO, VP ECMO.
Be ready for packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusion, if required.
Be ready to perform CPR/ACLS if/as required in case of emergency.
If the patient isn't on mechanical ventilation, be ready to manage airways in case of emergency.
Check the coagulation profile and increase anticoagulant dosing, if deemed necessary.
Proceed with Replacement
If cardiac arrest occurs during the procedure and EBF can be promptly restarted, carefully consider if adrenaline administration is advisable or could be delayed.
Sterile Operators
Disinfect the portion of the old drainage and return tubing which is going to be clamped and cut.
Allow the disinfection solution to act for enough time according to the solution which has been used.
Prepare the sterile field
Bring the sterile portion of the new circuit tubings on the field, then clamp and cut to the desired length.
If using new connectors, connect these to the drainage and return tubing.
Place two clamps approximately 15 cm (six inches) apart on both limbs of the old circuit to isolate.
Cut drainage and return lines between the clamps.
Make an air-free connection between the old and the new lines.
Double check:
Drainage with drainage line (blue markings)
Return with return line (red markings)
Remove all clamps apart from one on the return side.
Ask the ECMO specialist/perfusionist to restart the pump.
Check all connections for tightness and integrity, and secure all connections.
ECMO Specialist/Perfusionist
Note: These steps should be performed simultaneously for both roles.
If ready for clamping on the field, clamp the return line.
Go to 0 RPMs.
Clamp the drainage line.
Disconnect the gas line from the old circuit.
Connect gas line to the new circuit.
*OPTIONAL — If requested by sterile operators, fill the tubings after the clamps and the connectors using a line connected on the circuit.
Increase pump speed as requested by the team leader.
As the minimum RPMs are reached to prevent backflow (depending on IFUs - refer to Pumps) and remove the last clamp on the return line.
Refer to the Pump specifications.
Go back to previous RPMs settings if there are no signs of a return obstruction.
Go to Return Obstruction checklist.
Go back to previous FsO₂ settings.
Carefully increase sweep gas flow (SGF) considering enhanced ML function.
Dispose of the old circuit according to hospital protocol.
If a new ECMO machine was used, clean the one which was previously used according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Post-replacement Management
Strictly monitor the patient for signs of complications.
Adapt the ECMO settings as needed, considering the improved function of the new circuit.
Perform a full circuit assessment before leaving the patient.
Refer to the Circuit Monitoring checklist for more information.
Document the procedure in the patient's chart, including:
The reason for replacement
Time of the procedure
Circuit/connectors lot numbers
Complications encountered if any, operators
Report the procedure in the ELSO registry.

Mostly by hemodynamic and echocardiographic assessment

Moderate to severe RV dilation

PAPI = Pulmonary Artery Pulsatility Index = (systolic PAP - diastolic PAP) / CVP <0.9 indicates possible RV failure

Cannula
Dual-site single-lumen cannulas (VP ECMO configuration)
Left or right femoral vein multistage drainage cannula (21–25 Fr, 50–55 cm)

Return to pulmonary artery (1–2 cm beyond pulmonic valve)
Cannulation technique for VP and (dl)VP ECMO and initiation
Modified Seldinger technique
Usually access to right internal jugular vein (RIJV) or the left subclavian vein
8 Fr or 9 Fr introducer sheath placement
A balloon-tipped wedge pressure catheter is advanced through the sheath into the right pulmonary artery (PA)
Using transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or fluoroscopy guidance
A long 0.035-inch Lunderquist (Cook Medical) or Amplatz (Boston Scientific) extra stiff wire is positioned within the right PA through the balloon catheter
The balloon catheter and introducer sheath are then removed, while keeping the stiff wire properly positioned in the right PA.
Under fluoroscopic guidance, the entry site is progressively dilated to just below the necessary diameter for the chosen cannula
Again, take great care to maintain the position of the wire in the right PA.
The cannula then is inserted over the guidewire until the tip of the cannula is in the right PA. Once the cannula is inserted, the internal dilator is removed and both cannula ports are clamped.
A primed ECMO circuit may be wet-to-wet connected
The clamps are then carefully removed
Pump flow is gradually increased at the clinician’s judgment
The device is secured at the insertion site with care to avoid direct suturing to the cannula body, as this may cause cannula erosion
Suture rings are provided in the dual lumen cannula kits
Chest x-ray for cannula position verification
Perform a tansthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) to rule out complications

Perforation

title: Venopulmonary (VP) ECMO Weaning
content: This checklist should be adapted to align with institutional policies, specific patient conditions, and available resources.
keywords: VP ECMO; VP MANAGEMENT; ECMO; ECMO MANAGEMENT; VENOPULMONARY; WEANING; VP WEANING; ECMO WEANING

items.label: Background
Venopulmonary (VP) extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) supports both pulmonary and right ventricular (RV) functions
Utilization of this mode has been associated with improved outcomes
The peripheral VP ECMO mode has a variety of cannulation configurations
A single specialized dual-lumen cannula (ProtekDuo, Spectrum Medical)
Multiple single-lumen cannulas, or a combination of both dual- and single-lumen cannulas
The flexibility of VP ECMO allows for independent support of each organ system without needing to reconfigure cannulas
Weaning patients from VP ECMO requires careful assessment of both RV and lung recovery, which may occur at different rates.
Weaning methods are often poorly described or omitted in scientific manuscripts
The following is a detailed strategy for weaning patients with concomitant respiratory and RV failure from VP ECMO support
Weaning of VP ECMO
Assessing a patient’s readiness for ECMO weaning is conducted daily
VP ECMO weaning approach treats respiratory and RV support as separate entities
Before ECMO weaning, efforts are made to extubate patients
If extubation is impracticable, maintain recommended lung-protective mechanical ventilation settings
Start 2 phased weaning process
1st wean respiratory support
2nd wean RV support
Phase 1: Respiratory Support Weaning
Patients with concurrent RV and respiratory failure are first weaned from respiratory support, since respiratory failure may precipitate or exacerbate RV failure
Throughout the weaning of respiratory support, the ECMO pump flow is maintained at a rate that is adequate for providing full RV support
Arterial blood gases (ABGs) are monitored every 6 hours, or more frequently as clinically indicated
Guided by ABG values, employ stepwise reduction in sweep gas flow (SGF) by 1 L/min to maintain desired PH
Decrease sweep gas oxygen inlet oxygen fraction (FSO<sub>2</sub>) by 0.10 increments approximately every six hours.
Arterial blood gases are reassessed 30–45 min after each adjustment
With each reduction, ensure the patient sustains target respiratory parameters
Maintain acceptable pH and PaCO<sub>2 </sub>based on the patient’s clinical condition and work-of-breathing
Maintain an SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥92% or PaO<sub>2</sub> ≥70 mmHg

Once the SGF is 1 L/min and the FSO2 is 0.21, and the patient has maintained targetrespiratory parameters on these settings for up to 6 hours, perform an ECMO discontinuation trial by disconnecting the gas sources from the circuit (“off blender”) while continuing RV support
The patient can remain “off blender” as long as target respiratory parameters are maintained
If the patient cannot sustain these targets, respiratory ECMO support is resumed
If patient remains free from respiratory ECMO support for a continuous 24 hours the membrane lung (ML) may be removed from the circuit
Continuing RV support alone in a (dl)VxP or VxP configuration
Supplemental oxygen, mobilization, and clearing of respiratory secretions are employed to avoid the need for increased respiratory support
If escalation of respiratory support becomes necessary, a ML can be reintegrated into the extracorporeal circuit, or the patient may be reintubated if airway protection is required
Phase 2: Right Ventricular Support Weaning
Weaning from RV support is guided by improvements in cardiac function, especially RV performance.
All vasopressors should be off at this point
Maintain inotropic support depending on blood pressure (BP)
If mean arterial pressure (MAP) > 75 mmHg, start milrinone (0.125–0.5 mcg/kg/min)
If mean arterial pressure (MAP) < 65 mmHg, start epinephrine (0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min)
Gradually wean in pump flow by 0.25–0.5 L/min each day until a constant flow rate of 2 L/min is reached and tolerated for approximately 24 hours
Indicators are improved hemodynamics and organ function parameters
Central venous pressure (CVP) of less than 15 mmHg
MAP greater than or equal to 65 mmHg
Cardiac index (CI) greater than or equal to 2.2 L/min/m<sup>2</sup>
Normal lactate
Normalization or continued improvement in laboratory markers of organ function
Assess RV function by echocardiography (RV and LV dimension and interaction during flow weaning)
Maintain awareness of the strengths and limitations of assessed parameters based on image quality
When hemodynamic criteria are met, conduct a bedside “turn-down” test
During the bedside turn-down test, we methodically reduce pump flow over shorter time intervals while carefully monitoring the patient’s hemodynamic parameters after each reduction.
This practice typically involves the use of a Swan–Ganz or pulmonary wedge pressure catheter, for direct measurement of:
Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO<sub>2</sub>)
Assessment of RV hemodynamics, including the PA pulsatility index (PAPi).

In instances where the patient has recently undergone cardiothoracic surgery, the final decision regarding placement of an additional catheter in the PA is left to the surgeon’s discretion, particularly if there are concerns regarding the integrity of suture lines around the PA.
Before reducing pump flow to less than 2 L/min, it is imperative to ensure an activated clotting time (ACT) of at least 250 seconds to mitigate the risk of thrombosis within the circuit.
If anticoagulation is contraindicated or an adequate ACT level unattainable, further reductions in pump flow are not pursued

The authors practice is to document baseline hemodynamic values when pump flow is at 2 L/min, then reduce the flow incrementally to 1.5, 1, and 0.5 L/min, before completely stopping flow by applying a clamp to the circuit tubing on both the drainage and return limbs. Pump flow is not stopped for longer than two minutes.
At each flow level, RV function and dimension by echocardiogram, hemodynamic parameters including CVP, MAP, CI, and PAPi are assessed

In the absence of a Swan–Ganz or pulmonary wedge pressure catheter, CVP and MAP are measured and integrated with echocardiographic findings. CI may be calculated obtaining LVOT dimension and velocity, since the LV can only eject what the RV is pumping forward

If RV function remains acceptable during the bedside turn down test without a need for more than minimal inotropic or vasopressor support, RV support is terminated, and the patient is decannulated at the bedside.
Should weaning not be tolerated, multidisciplinary evaluation for durable support or heart transplantation is initiated.

Special Considerations
Right ventricular recovery before respiratory recovery:

When RV function improves rapidly and significantly before respiratory function, clinicians might consider transitioning from VP to VV ECMO. However, the authors usual practice is to continue using VP ECMO, as this strategy has proven effective
First, the pathophysiological mechanisms contributing to RV failure often persist in patients with respiratory failure, even when using VV ECMO

Second, there is no evidence that switching from VP to VV ECMO is superior, and some studies suggest VP ECMO may provide benefits over VV ECMO, particularly in patients with respiratory failure due to COVID-19
Maintaining VP ECMO avoids additional procedures that increase both risk and cost
Clinicians may choose to switch from VP to VV ECMO if a cannula in the PA causes adverse effects that can best be addressed by reconfiguration to VV ECMO
If clinicians decide to remove RV support by switching from VP to VV ECMO first, they must closely monitor RV function
Concomitant Transvalvular Left Ventricular Support Device
Using VP ECMO in conjunction with a transvalvular left ventricular support (TVLS) device is a viable option for combined respiratory and biventricular support
In cases where patients are supported by both VP ECMO and a TVLS device, the approach to weaning from VP ECMO remains consistent:
Start by weaning from respiratory support, followed by RV support
This can occur independently of weaning from the TVLS device
If a patient is first liberated from VP ECMO while continuing support with the TVLS device, close monitoring of RV function is essential
Maintain a low threshold for employing interventions to support RV function
